item.title: Rebuildable Airflow: snapshot the running container, redeploy with a rollback
item.author: william
item.description:
Update 2026-11-11 17:30: image tags are now the build time, yyyymmddTHHMMSS (e.g. airflow:20261111T172041), so two builds on the same day no longer collide, and ./run.sh with no tag lists what’s available. The outputs below are from the first build, which still used a plain date tag, 20261111. The downloadable scripts are the current versions.

The outage postmortem had one recurring theme: every time someone rebuilt the Airflow container by hand, it came back missing something. A mount, the concurrency settings, the plugin, the registry login. The image was whatever someone last typed, and the settings that mattered lived only in a running container.

So the same afternoon I wrote three small scripts. build.airflow.sh turns the running container into an image tagged with its build time (airflow:20261111T172041), pushes it, and saves a tarball. run.sh recreates the container from that tag and checks it’s actually healthy, or puts the old one back. restart.sh runs inside the container and keeps the scheduler and webserver up. From the 170 entries in docker diff, the image keeps 13 files (172K). A redeploy is healthy about 15 s after the new container starts, and a failed one rolls back in 1 s.

item.title: Thin, pale monospace in Chrome: a Powerline font config was vetoing every good mono font
item.author: william
item.description:
Two pages I look at every day had the same problem: monospace text that was too thin and pale to read comfortably. One was the log viewer in our Airflow 2.7 web UI, the other the dark theme of an internal Tabler dashboard. In both, Chrome was drawing the text in Courier New, a hairline font, even though both pages list four or five better fonts before it.

The cause was a fontconfig file from the fonts-powerline package, installed in 2019. It puts the symbols-only “PowerlineSymbols” font in front of most monospace families, and Chrome then refuses every one of them. A one-rule fontconfig file fixed it.

item.title: One night, one dead disk: an Airflow trading-host outage and what it taught me
item.author: william
item.description:
Update 2026-11-11: the “a restart is a procedure, not a command” advice below is now three scripts: a dated image built from the running container, a redeploy that refuses while tasks run and rolls back on failure, and a supervisor inside the container. See Rebuildable Airflow.

At 19:56 one evening, a 21.8 TB data disk on our Airflow host started throwing I/O errors. By 21:37 someone had pointed Docker at a fresh, empty data directory to get things running again. That one change, made under pressure and never written down, turned into five separate incidents by 09:30 the next morning: a message broker that vanished, a missing mount, concurrency limits back at their defaults, live-trading processes Airflow no longer knew about, and two restarts that orphaned every live trade.

Everything was back by 10:08. This post is the timeline, the root cause of each problem, how each was fixed (including the 1.5-minute outage I caused myself while fixing it), and what I would change so this can’t happen the same way again.

item.title: Fixing duplicated tmux status bars and missing icons in Termius on iPhone
item.author: william
item.description:
My tmux status bar looked fine on Linux, but connecting to the same session from Termius on my iPhone left repeated copies of the bar at the bottom of the screen. Moving it to the top was a useful workaround. I wanted to keep it at the bottom and keep the desktop’s colors and useful widgets.

The fix was a compact renderer for clients below 100 columns, followed by a targeted replacement for an icon the phone could not render. This extends my one-job status renderer: the phone still uses one status job, and a desktop attached to the same session keeps its full layout. The app is Termius, although I initially called it Terminus.

item.title: Profiling zsh: a Python plugin was adding 190 ms to every command
item.author: william
item.description:
After fixing tmux, I looked at the shell running inside it. My zsh config had grown over a few years to about 30 plugins and Oh My Zsh snippets on top of zinit and Powerlevel10k. It felt a little heavy, but nothing stood out.

Measured properly, it was slow in three separate ways, each with its own cause:

before after
startup to a usable shell 267 ms 101 ms
added to every command 188 ms 3 ms
added to every prompt 15 ms 4 ms

This post covers how I measured each one, the fixes, and how I checked that the fixes didn’t change anything else. That check caught two mistakes of my own.

item.title: tmux lag, round 2: every status-bar fork froze the server for 30 ms
item.author: william
item.description:
Update 2026-10-09: I extended this renderer for a 71-column iPhone client: compact text stopped duplicated bottom status rows while keeping the desktop colors and widgets. See the Termius on iPhone follow-up.

Two days after the last fix, my tmux was laggy again, and the server was back at about a quarter of a CPU core. The culprit was the same as last time: the status bar’s #() jobs. This time, though, the number of jobs wasn’t the problem. Each one had become slow, because every job is a fork of the whole tmux server and my server had grown to 1.5 GB.

This post covers how I measured it, where the 1.5 GB came from (mostly the scrollback of three panes), and the fixes. One of them corrects a claim in my previous post.

item.title: Why my tmux was laggy: the status bar was forking a 1.2 GB server 24 times a second
item.author: william
item.description:
Update 2026-10-02: two days later the lag was back. Each fork of the server had become slow (~30 ms), and one claim below was wrong: passing #{E:#{@quote_cond}} into the job does not work, because tmux does not apply strftime inside a #() command. See round 2.

My tmux had started to feel sluggish. Nothing was broken, it just felt heavy. It turned out the tmux server was using about a third of a CPU core all the time, and nearly all of that went on the status bar. Part of the cost came from the clock workaround in my previous post.

This post covers how I tracked it down, including two wrong guesses, and the fix, which brought the server from ~35% CPU to ~4% without restarting it.

item.title: Installing Clash Verge Rev on Ubuntu 20.04 / Mint 20 — and upgrading its mihomo core
item.author: william
item.description:
Clash Verge Rev is a desktop GUI for the mihomo proxy core (formerly Clash Meta). It is the maintained fork of the original Clash Verge, which was abandoned in 2023. If a tutorial tells you to use zzzgydi/clash-verge, skip it.

On a modern Ubuntu, installing it takes one command. On my Mint 20.3 (focal, glibc 2.31), the latest .deb would not install, and the failed attempt left apt in a broken state. Unlike Claude Desktop and ChatGPT Desktop, there is no clean way to patch around it this time. The practical fix is to run the last 1.x GUI with an up-to-date core.

item.title: Linux 时区、系统时间与 tmux 状态栏时间不一致的排查
item.author: william
item.description:
我把 Linux 的时区设成 Asia/Tokyo，又手动设置了系统时间，但 tmux 右侧状态栏仍慢一个小时。例如，系统显示 14:37 JST，tmux 却显示 13:37 CST。问题不在 timedatectl set-time：一个早已启动的 tmux server 仍按旧时区格式化状态栏。

2
3

sudo timedatectl set-timezone Asia/Tokyo
sudo timedatectl set-ntp false
# aligned to real Asia/Shanghai time
timedatectl set-time "2026-09-26 15:33:00"
